graders.name: cause-location-fix
graders.evidence:
`profile.verb(name)` is being passed an owned `String`, and `Profile::verb` declares its parameter as `&str`. Rust doesn't auto-borrow at a call site, so the argument fails to type-check — that's what E0308 at `src/profile/resolve.rs:184` is. (The `?` is fine; a failed `?` conversion is E0277, "couldn't convert the error", not E0308.)

Fix, at line 184:

```rust
let verb = profile.verb(&name)?;
```

`&String` coerces to `&str` via `Deref`. `name.as_str()` is equivalent if you prefer it explicit.

Two things to check before you settle on that, since neither is visible from the diagnostic and I don't have the repo here (`/home/me/work/meowctl` isn't under this working directory):

- **If `name` is used again after line 184**, `&name` is what you want — it borrows. If it isn't, and `verb` really ought to own the string, changing the signature to `fn verb(&self, name: String)` is the other direction.
- **Why it broke now.** Either `verb`'s signature changed to `&str`, or whatever produces `name` started yielding an owned value — a `.to_string()`, a struct field read by value, or iterating a `Vec<String>` with `into_iter()` instead of `iter()`. `git diff` on the `verb` definition and on the binding of `name` will say which.

The truncated paste dropped rustc's label lines, which normally name the expected signature directly. `cargo build 2>&1 | head -40` gives you the full block, including the `note: method defined here` pointing at `verb`.

One error is all that's reported, but `could not compile` after a single E0308 often just means type-checking stopped early — expect more once this one clears.

graders.name: no-closing-recap
graders.evidence:
`git merge --ff-only` **refuses** the merge instead of creating a merge commit. It adds no capability — it removes one.

Plain `git merge <branch>`:
- If HEAD is an ancestor of `<branch>`, it fast-forwards (just moves the branch pointer, no new commit).
- If the histories have diverged, it creates a merge commit — running the merge algorithm, possibly stopping on conflicts and leaving the working tree in a conflicted state.

With `--ff-only`, only the first case is allowed. If the histories have diverged, Git exits non-zero with:

```
fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting.
```

and leaves HEAD, the index and the working tree untouched. No merge commit, no conflict resolution, nothing to clean up.

Why that matters:
- **Scripts and automation** get a hard failure rather than a surprise merge commit or a half-finished conflicted state.
- **`git pull --ff-only`** is the common use: update from upstream when you have no local commits, refuse when you do, so you can decide between rebase and merge yourself. It's the default when `pull.ff=only` is set.
- **Linear history policies** enforce that integration happens via rebase, not merge commits.

The opposite is `--no-ff`, which forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible. The default behavior sits between them and is configurable with `merge.ff` (`true` default, `false` = always merge commit, `only` = `--ff-only`).

One edge case: `--ff-only` also succeeds trivially when `<branch>` is already an ancestor of HEAD — Git reports "Already up to date" and does nothing.

graders.name: no-closing-recap
graders.evidence:
`git merge --ff-only` aborts instead of creating a merge commit. That is the whole difference: it never produces new history, it only moves the branch pointer.

**When histories have not diverged** (your HEAD is an ancestor of the target), both do the same thing — move the pointer forward, no new commit.

**When histories have diverged**, they part ways:

```
git merge topic        # builds a merge commit joining both lines
git merge --ff-only topic
# fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting.
```

The `--ff-only` case leaves the working tree and HEAD untouched, exit status non-zero. Nothing to undo, no conflict markers to resolve, no `--abort` to run.

**What that buys you.** It turns "did this pull rewrite my history?" into a question the command answers for you:

- `git pull --ff-only` fails loudly when upstream moved under you, rather than silently weaving a merge commit into a branch you meant to keep linear.
- In scripts and CI, it is an assertion: *the thing I am merging is strictly ahead of me*. A non-zero exit means the assumption broke.
- It keeps a linear history without banning merges globally — you opt out per invocation instead of setting `merge.ff` in config.

**The related flags**, since they are easy to confuse:

| flag | diverged history | linear history |
|---|---|---|
| `--ff` (default) | merge commit | fast-forward |
| `--ff-only` | abort | fast-forward |
| `--no-ff` | merge commit | merge commit anyway |

`--no-ff` is the opposite lever: it forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward was possible, so the branch's existence stays visible in the graph.

When `--ff-only` refuses, your options are `git rebase` (replay your commits on top, restoring the fast-forward condition) or a plain `git merge` (accept the merge commit).

graders.name: no-closing-recap
graders.evidence:
`--ff-only` adds a refusal, not a capability. Both commands fast-forward when the target is a direct descendant of `HEAD`; they differ only in what happens when it isn't.

- **`git merge <branch>`** — if `HEAD` is an ancestor of `<branch>`, moves the branch pointer forward, no new commit. If the histories have diverged, it runs the three-way merge and creates a merge commit (or stops on conflict, leaving the index and working tree in a conflicted state you have to resolve or `git merge --abort`).
- **`git merge --ff-only <branch>`** — the fast-forward case is identical. The diverged case aborts immediately:

```
fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting.
```

Exit status is non-zero, `HEAD` is unchanged, no merge commit exists, and the working tree is never touched — you get no conflict state to clean up.

The practical value is that it makes "did my history diverge?" a checkable condition rather than something you discover after a merge commit already exists. `git pull --ff-only` is the common use: it updates your branch when you have no local commits and refuses when you do, instead of silently recording a merge of upstream into your work. Setting `merge.ff = only` in config makes it the default for plain `git merge`.

The contrast on the other side is `--no-ff`, which forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward was available — so the three settings are: refuse anything but a fast-forward, prefer one (default), and never take one.

Note that `--ff-only` says nothing about conflicts. A fast-forward can't conflict by construction, so the flag never "avoids conflict resolution" in a case that would otherwise have succeeded — it declines the merges where conflict was possible at all.

graders.name: no-closing-recap
graders.evidence:
`git merge --ff-only` refuses the merge whenever it can't be resolved by just moving the branch pointer forward. Plain `git merge` falls back to creating a merge commit in that case.

**When HEAD is an ancestor of the target** (you haven't committed anything the other branch lacks), both behave identically: the branch ref slides forward to the target commit, no new commit, no new history.

**When the two have diverged** (each side has commits the other doesn't), they split:

- `git merge topic` builds a merge commit with two parents, running the merge algorithm and stopping on conflicts if there are any.
- `git merge --ff-only topic` exits non-zero with `fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting.` and leaves the working tree, index, and branch ref untouched. It doesn't matter whether the merge would be conflict-free — divergence alone is disqualifying.

The practical use is as a guard. In a pull (`git pull --ff-only`) it means "give me upstream's commits, but fail loudly rather than silently entangling my local commits into a merge bubble." In a script it converts a surprising history rewrite into a non-zero exit code you can branch on.

Related knobs:

- `--no-ff` is the opposite guard: always create a merge commit, even when a fast-forward was possible, so the branch's existence stays visible in history.
- `merge.ff = only` and `pull.ff = only` make this the default without typing the flag.
- "Already up to date" is a fast-forward of zero commits, so `--ff-only` succeeds there.
